content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: `needs` expresses job dependency relationships and allows a downstream job to read the result and declared outputs of its prerequisites. Use `needs` for dependencies, matrices for controlled combinations, conditions for deliberate branching, and concurrency/timeouts to prevent stale or unbounded work. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: The needs keyword
items.text: Declare job dependencies with `needs` and read prerequisite results or outputs through `needs.<job>`. Separate jobs do not share a runner workspace automatically.

items.title: Handling failed and skipped dependencies
items.text: For handling failed and skipped dependencies, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

content_blocks.code:
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Validate input and exit status"
  report:
    needs: validate
    if: ${{ always() }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Inspect the dependency result before acting"
content_blocks.expected_output: The reporting job waits for the validation job and runs even after it finishes; real cleanup/reporting logic should inspect `needs.validate.result` before making decisions.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to job dependencies. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain job dependencies, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Express dependencies and parallel work as a clear job graph with bounded execution and failure behavior.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: `needs` expresses job dependency relationships and allows a downstream job to read the result and declared outputs of its prerequisites. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
